title: Demand Shepherding and Cost Gating — Dedicated Capacity PRD (Draft)
content:
Context:

This doc is an engineering-forward PRD proposing a new surface for managing sudden demand spikes on Dedicated capacity: a Demand Shepherding layer plus a Cost Gating primitive. The goal is to let product teams preserve latency SLOs for critical routes, absorb microbursts without expensive overprovisioning, and give tenants transparent, predictable controls over burst economics and isolation boundaries.

Why this feels different:
- Most prior drafts center on elastic pools, credit tokens, or lane-based throttles. Demand Shepherding reframes the problem as active traffic shaping at the ingress boundary with explicit cost signals and a lightweight queued buffer that cooperates with autoscalers and tenant isolation lanes.
- We want to reduce the need to pre-buy large reserved headroom while providing operational guardrails for tail-latency sensitive workloads.

Problem statement:
- Tenants experience unpredictable microbursts that either cause latency SLO violations or force expensive permanent headroom reservations.
- Current Dedicated configs allow soft-bursting and eviction but lack:
  1) a simple way to steer non-critical requests into a managed buffer,
  2) tenant-facing cost caps that prevent runaway spend during bursts,
  3) a predictable downgrade path that preserves core user journeys.

Goals (measurable):
- Reduce transient SLO breaches during microbursts by 60% for guarded routes within 3 months of rollout.
- Lower average committed headroom for participating tenants by 15% (simulated/observed) without increased error rates.
- Provide tenant controls: burst budget per billing period + per-minute cost gate with transparent billing preview.

Non-goals:
- Replacing existing autoscaler heuristics entirely. Demand Shepherding *cooperates* with autoscalers.
- Complex per-model compilation/quantization changes. This is an ingress and policy layer.

User personas and stories:
- Platform engineer (high SLO): "Keep my chat completions within 150ms at p95 even if the rest of the org runs heavy batch embeddings."
- Growth-app engineer (cost sensitive): "I want my staging environment to absorb short bursts without me getting a massive invoice; queue lower-priority requests with explicit cost caps."
- Operator oncall: "When a demand spike hits, I want a clear trace showing what was shepherded, what triggered cost gates, and a safe manual override."

Product approach (high level):
1) Ingress shepherd: lightweight per-route policy that classifies requests into priority buckets (critical, opportunistic, background). Critical flows bypass the shepherd buffer and hit serving lanes; opportunistic/background can be queued, deferred, or rerouted.
2) Elastic side-queue (shepherd queue): a short, bounded queue with time-based decay and KV-hinting for prefix reuse. Not intended for long waits — typical TTLs < 3s.
3) Cost gating tokens: small budget tokens allocated per-tenant and per-route that gate how much opportunistic work may execute on dedicated GPUs. Tokens can be numeric $-equivalent or token-count equivalent of GPU-seconds. Exceeding the gate flips behavior to deferred/retry-with-backoff or to a lower-fidelity model.
4) Isolation lanes mapping: shepherd integrates with lane assignments (latency lanes, economical lanes). When capacity pressure is observed, the shepherd will rehome opportunistic requests to lower-cost lanes or enqueue them.
5) Autoscaler handshake: shepherd exposes a short-term demand forecast signal and a drain suggestion API to the autoscaler so scaling decisions can consider buffered demand rather than immediate failovers.

Key components and interactions:
- Client SDK hints: clients can tag calls with "execution-priority" and optional "cost-willingness" (e.g., willing_to_pay_premium=true). These hints are purely advisory but influence shepherd decisions.
- Route policy config: per-route YAML in account config (console + API) with fields: priority_class, max_shepherd_queue_ms, cost_gate_cap, fallback_action (reject|queue|degrade|route-to-hosted).
- Shepherd controller: central small service in control plane per-region that evaluates queue depth, token budgets, lane occupancy, and emits routing decisions.
- Token ledger: per-tenant ledger that debits token budget when opportunistic workloads are admitted; supports borrowing (soft) with caps and expiration.
- Observability: new metrics (shepherd.admit_rate, costgate.blocked_minutes, queue_latency_histogram, token_drawdown_pct) and tracing spans for shepherded requests.

Behavioral policies (examples):
- Default: critical bypass, opportunistic queued up to 1200 requests or 2s TTL whichever first, background dropped with 202 + retry-after.
- Aggressive-cost-gate: if per-minute token usage > cap, accept only critical requests and route redispatched opportunistic traffic to hosted fallback.
- Low-latency-favor: maintain p95 target by dynamically shrinking queue TTL (from 2s to 250ms) when lane latency approaches 90% of SLO.

Autoscaler integration specifics:
- Forecast feed: shepherd computes a short-horizon expected admitted QPS (1–30s) and exposes it through a dataplane endpoint (protocol v0.1). Autoscaler reads this signal and applies configured smoothing (alpha) before making node-level decisions.
- Warm pool guidance: shepherd can request a warmpool of N slots for a tenant when queued admission exceeds threshold X for more than Y seconds. 
- Backoff loop: if autoscaler cannot provision, shepherd escalates to cost gating and fallback rules (route-to-hosted or degrade model).

Cost gating and billing model (draft):
- Two dimensions: committed base (monthly reserved) + burst budget (prepaid or pay-as-you-go).
- Cost gate token semantics: 1 token == 1 GPU-second at tenant's selected fidelity profile. Console displays token burn-rate estimate per-route in dollars.
- Billing preview: before exceeding burst budget, system emits an alert + invoice preview; tenant can opt into auto-topup or have requests rejected until next billing period.

Isolation and fairness:
- Soft partition: cost gating ensures that noisy tenants cannot exceed per-period budgets; when exhausted, shepherd routes tenant traffic to lower-fidelity model lanes or enqueues/rejects.
- Fair admission: when multiple tenants contend the same opportunistic lane, admission probability is proportional to remaining token balance * priority_weight.
- Emergency isolation: operator-run escalation that shorts all opportunistic admissions for selected tenant(s) for X minutes, with automated unfreeze after cooldown.

Operational runbook (high level):
- On spike detection: check shepherd.admit_rate, token drawdown, lane occupancy. If admit_rate >> baseline and queue_latency rising -> trigger warmpool request, notify ops channel.
- When cost gate trips: auto-send invoice-preview and open a temporary mitigation ticket; apply fallback_action in route config.
- Post-incident: collect traces; compute percentage of requests shepherded vs served. Evaluate cost impact and SLO impact.

Metrics/SLOs to track:
- p95 latency for critical routes (must not increase > 10% post rollout)
- shepherd.admit_rate and queue_latency_p99
- token_burn_rate and fraction of tenants hitting gates
- fraction_of_requests_routed_to_hosted_fallback

Rollout plan (phased):
1) Internal beta: product & infra teams, synthetic microburst tests, verify autoscaler handshake (2 weeks).
2) Early access: 5 tenants opt-in with console toggles, telemetry enabled, manual review of cost previews (6 weeks).
3) Gradual rollout: enable default policy for new Dedicated tenants; existing tenants must opt-in (3 months).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Shepherding adds latency to opportunistic requests and could complicate billing disputes. Mitigation: strict TTLs, clear in-console cost previews, and preflight simulation tools for tenants.
- Risk: Autoscaler misreads shepherd forecasts and over/under provisions. Mitigation: smoothing heuristics, conservative warmpool defaults, and a read-only dry-run mode for autoscaler during initial weeks.

Open questions (needs engineering input):
- Exact token granularity and how to translate different model fidelities to GPU-seconds reliably.
- Side-effects of queueing on KV/prefix cache hit rates (will shepherding harm prefix reuse?).
- Failure modes for the shepherd controller — how to fail-open vs fail-closed safely.

Next steps / immediate action items:
- (Aisha) Draft API schema for per-route YAML and console UI mockups (1 week).
- (Marcus/Infra) Prototype short-horizon forecast endpoint and basic token ledger in a staging region (2 weeks).
- (Elena/Telemetry) Add shepherd metrics to telemetry backlog and a dashboard template for early access tenants (1 week).
- (Samir/Ops) Prepare runbook templates and cost-preview email templates (1 week).

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally a lightweight, operational-first PRD — focus feedback on failure modes, billing semantics, and the autoscaler handshake. The aim is to keep the serving runtime unchanged and implement most of the logic in the control plane and at the ingress proxies.
